Submission: October 28, 2026 (External Design Review)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents Board B: Cap / Lid Sensing, my subsystem of Team 102's Automatic Pill Dispenser for EGR 304 (Embedded Systems Design) at Arizona State University. It collects the block diagram, component selection, bill of materials, schematic and power budget for the board, so a reader can see what the board does, why each part was chosen, and how it connects to the rest of the dispenser.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: Missed doses and accidental double doses are a common problem for people managing daily medication. Team 102 (Arya Padiyar, Natalia Diaz, Samandar Kholmuminov and Taylor Calli) is building an automatic pill dispenser that presents the right dose at the right time and makes it hard to take an extra or early dose. A central hub board coordinates four subsystem boards, each built around a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano with its own sensor or actuator and analog signal chain: a carousel drive with jam detection, optical dose-confirmation sensing, audible alerts, and lid sensing. The boards share data over an 8-pin ribbon cable.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
I designed Board B, which tells the hub when the pill bottle cap is opened. A photoresistor under the cap is dark while the cap is closed; when the cap opens, light reaches it and the divider voltage rises. An MCP6004 op-amp chain amplifies and filters that signal for the PIC's ADC, and an LM393 comparator gives a clean open/closed signal. Board B reports LID_OPEN, LID_FAULT and a heartbeat to the hub, receives DOSE_READY, and also has a UART link. It runs from a 9 V wall adapter through an L7805CV regulator.

Rev 3 (October 27, 2026): on the teaching team's recommendation, the original Hall-effect sensor and cap magnet were replaced by a photoresistor. Every page below has been updated to match.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Arya Padiyar — Team 102: Automatic Pill Dispenser Subsystem: Board B — Cap / Lid Sensing (Rev 3)

This block diagram shows how my subsystem, Board B, is laid out and how it connects to the team's hub board.

  • Power levels: A 9V wall adapter enters through a DC barrel jack, then a 500 mA fuse and a 1N5819 reverse-polarity diode. An L7805CV linear regulator steps it down to 5V, which feeds the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano's VBUS through jumper JP1. The Nano's on-board LDO supplies 3.3V (VTG) to the sensor, op-amp, comparator and all logic, so no signal can go above the PIC's 3.3V pin limit.
  • Sensor: A photoresistor (the same light-dependent resistor from our Resistive Sensor Lab) sits under the bottle cap in a voltage divider with R19 = 3.9 kΩ. With the cap closed the sensor is dark (high resistance, low voltage). When the cap opens, light reaches it and the divider voltage rises.
  • Signal chain: The divider output goes two ways. One path runs through an MCP6004 non-inverting amplifier, a low-pass filter (fc ≈ 15.9 Hz) and a unity-gain buffer into the ADC on RA0, so I can read the actual light level. The other path goes to an LM393 comparator, which gives a clean open/closed digital signal on RB0.
  • Outputs and debug: A red lid status LED on RC5, a yellow heartbeat LED on RF2, a debug push button on RD3, and a green power-good LED on the 5V rail.
  • Team connections: Board B connects to the hub (J2) through 8-pin ribbon connector J1. I use pins 1–5 and 7 for signals, pin 8 for GND, and pin 6 is spare.

docs.title: What changed since the last version
docs.text: Change Why Replaced the linear Hall-effect sensor (DRV5055) and cap magnet with a photoresistor + 3.9 kΩ (R19) voltage divider Recommended by the teaching team (Zane Reynolds and Dr. Nichols, Oct 21). It still meets the analog-sensor requirement and works the same way (analog value → ADC + comparator), but it doesn't need a magnet mounted in the cap. It also reuses a circuit we already built and characterized in the light lab. Added the MCP6004 signal-conditioning block (amplifier, low-pass filter, buffer) The schematic already had this stage; the diagram now matches it. Added input protection (fuse + reverse diode) and JP1 to VBUS Matches the schematic's power section. Added UART_RX (pin 4) and UART_TX (pin 7) to J1, the heartbeat LED, the debug button and the power-good LED Matches the team pinout and the debug features in the schematic. Removed the power arrows Power is shown by the dashed supply-domain boxes, as the block diagram checklist requires.

docs.title: How I structured the diagram
docs.text: I grouped every block by the supply rail it runs on (9V, 5V, 3.3V dashed boxes) so the power path reads left to right: wall adapter → protection → regulator → Nano. The sensing path then reads left to right along the top (light → divider → conditioning → MCU), and everything that leaves the board goes straight down to J1, so each ribbon pin lines up with the MCU pin that drives it. Arrows always point at the receiving block, which makes the direction of each team signal obvious during review.

docs.title: How it meets the product requirements
docs.text:
• Detect when the cap is opened: the divider voltage rises sharply when light reaches the sensor. From my light-lab measurements (46.3 kΩ covered, 11.07 kΩ low light, 1.54 kΩ room light), the divider gives about 0.26 V with the cap closed and 0.86–2.37 V with the cap open on the 3.3 V rail.
  • Analog signal chain: RA0 reads the conditioned light level, so firmware can tune the open/closed threshold and flag LID_FAULT when the reading is outside the expected range (for example, stuck at the 3.3 V rail).
  • Reliable digital state: the LM393 with hysteresis gives the hub a clean LID_OPEN signal without chatter at the threshold.
  • Safe logic levels: every analog part runs from 3.3 V, so nothing can exceed the PIC's pin limits.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Arya Padiyar | Team 102 | Board B: Cap / Lid Sensing

Board B detects when the pill bottle cap is opened. A photoresistor under the cap sits in the dark while the cap is closed; when the cap opens, light reaches it, its resistance drops and the divider voltage rises. An MCP6004 op-amp chain conditions that voltage for the PIC's ADC, an LM393 comparator turns it into a clean open/closed signal, and a linear regulator supplies the board from an external wall supply. The microcontroller (PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano) was selected by the course and is not compared here.

Rev 3 update (Oct 27): the lid sensor changed from a DRV5055 Hall-effect sensor + cap magnet to a photoresistor. The teaching team (Zane Reynolds, after discussing it with Dr. Nichols) recommended the photoresistor because it meets the analog-sensor requirement, works the same way (analog value into the ADC and the comparator), and does not need a magnet in the cap. It is also the sensor we already built and characterized in the Resistive Sensor Lab. The Hall sensor is kept below as Option 3 to show why it was replaced.

docs.title: 1. Lid Sensor (Light Sensor)
docs.text:
Subsystem: Board B – Cap / Lid Sensing

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.CdS photoresistor (LDR), 5 mm, e.g. Advanced Photonix PDV-P8001, in a divider with a 3.9 kΩ resistor$1.42/each (lab kit part used for testing)PDV-P8001 at Mouser · datasheet * Already characterized in our Resistive Sensor Lab: 46.3 kΩ covered, 11.07 kΩ low light, 1.54 kΩ room light, 66.5 Ω bright light* With R19 = 3.9 kΩ on 3.3 V the divider gives 0.26 V with the cap closed and 0.86–2.37 V with it open, a large, easy-to-detect step that never exceeds the PIC's 3.3 V ADC input* Gives an analog signal, so it meets the project's analog signal-chain requirement* No magnet or extra part in the cap; two leads, no polarity, fits the AP_R_LDR 5 mm footprint already in our library * Responds to room light, so it cannot tell open from closed in a dark room (handled in firmware by flagging LID_FAULT when the reading never changes)* Slow response (55 ms rise, 20 ms fall at 10 lux for the PDV-P8001), which is fine for a cap but slow for fast events* Large part-to-part spread (3–11 kΩ at 10 lux), so the threshold has to be set from measured values, not the datasheet alone Solution Pros Cons Option 2.Vishay TEPT5700 ambient-light phototransistor (5 mm T-1¾) with a load resistor$1.05/eachTEPT5700 at Mouser · datasheet * Spectral response matched to the human eye (peak 570 nm), so it reacts to normal room light like the photoresistor* Much faster than a CdS cell and with very low dark current (3 nA typical)* Same 5 mm through-hole style, easy to mount under the cap * Output is a small current (5.2–24 µA at 20 lux), so it needs a large load resistor or a transimpedance stage before the ADC* Polarized part (collector/emitter), so it is easier to install backwards* Not something we have characterized yet, so the threshold and gain would have to be designed from scratch Solution Pros Cons Option 3.TI DRV5055A1QLPG linear Hall-effect sensor + magnet in the cap (previous design, Rev 2)$0.77/eachDRV5055A1QLPG at Mouser * Not affected by room light, so it works in the dark* Ratiometric analog output that runs from 3.3 V* Can detect a missing magnet as a fault * Needs a magnet glued into every cap and the magnet's distance and orientation have to be controlled* Signal is small at 3.3 V (60 mV/mT), so the gain stage has to be tuned to the magnet* The teaching team recommended replacing it with the photoresistor for this project

Choice: Option 1: CdS photoresistor (light-lab part) with a 3.9 kΩ divider resistor

Rationale: The photoresistor gives the biggest, cleanest signal for the least hardware. We already measured it, so R19 was chosen from real data: the geometric mean of the low-light and room-light readings, √(11.07k × 1.54k) ≈ 4.1 kΩ, rounded to the standard 3.9 kΩ, which gives the widest voltage swing between those two conditions. With the cap closed the divider sits at 0.26 V, and any normal room light pushes it to 0.86 V or more, so a 0.54 V comparator threshold has margin on both sides. The phototransistor would need an extra current-to-voltage stage, and the Hall sensor needs a magnet in the cap, which is the main reason the teaching team recommended the switch. The one weakness, a dark room, is covered in firmware: if the cap is reported closed for a full dose window while DOSE_READY is active, Board B raises LID_FAULT so the hub can still alert the user.

docs.title: 2. Comparator
docs.text:
Subsystem: Board B – Cap / Lid Sensing

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.TI LM393P dual voltage comparator (PDIP-8)$0.53/eachLM393P at Mouser * Operates from 2 V to 30 V, so it runs from the same 3.3 V rail as the sensor divider* Open-collector output is pulled up to 3.3 V, so the signal into the PIC (RB0) is always at a safe logic level* Dual comparator in a PDIP-8 through-hole package that is easy to hand-solder* Low supply current (0.45 mA typical, 1 mA max at 5 V) and made by several manufacturers, so it is easy to source * Input common-mode range only reaches VCC - 1.5 V (about 1.8 V on a 3.3 V supply), so the switching threshold must sit below 1.8 V* Needs an external pull-up resistor on the output, plus feedback resistors to add hysteresis* Rated for 0 °C to 70 °C only, which is fine indoors but narrower than the other options Solution Pros Cons Option 2.Microchip MCP6541-I/P push-pull comparator (PDIP-8)$0.54/eachMCP6541-I/P at Mouser * Rail-to-rail inputs and output, so the threshold can be anywhere in the 0 V to 3.3 V range* Push-pull output drives the PIC input directly with no pull-up resistor* Very low quiescent current (about 600 nA typical)* PDIP-8 through-hole package that is easy to hand-solder * Single comparator per package, so a second channel would need another IC* Supply is limited to 1.6 V to 5.5 V, which gives less flexibility than the LM393* Push-pull output cannot be pulled up to a different logic level or wired together with other outputs Solution Pros Cons Option 3.Custom: Microchip MCP6002-I/P op-amp wired as a Schmitt-trigger comparator (PDIP-8)$0.45/eachMCP6002-I/P at Mouser * Threshold and hysteresis are set by resistors, so they can be tuned to the magnet distance in our cap* Rail-to-rail input and output and a 1.8 V to 6 V supply range, so it runs from the 3.3 V rail* Same Microchip MCP600x op-amp family used in our resistive sensor lab, so the team already knows the part * Op-amps are not designed to run in saturation; their slow recovery and 0.6 V/µs slew rate give slower, less clean edges than a true comparator* Needs more external resistors to design, place, and debug* No built-in hysteresis, so a wrong resistor value can make the output chatter when the cap is near the threshold

Choice: Option 1: TI LM393P dual voltage comparator

Rationale: The LM393 meets every Board B requirement once the threshold is kept inside its input range. On a 3.3 V supply its input common-mode range reaches about 1.8 V. The photoresistor divider sits at 0.26 V with the cap closed and 0.86–2.37 V with it open, so the threshold is set to 0.54 V (R10 = 51 kΩ, R11 = 10 kΩ), well inside that range and with margin on both sides. 10 kΩ / 470 kΩ positive feedback adds about 69 mV of hysteresis so the output does not chatter when the cap is half open. The open-collector output with a pull-up to 3.3 V guarantees a safe logic level on RB0. Several manufacturers make the LM393, which protects the build schedule from stock shortages. The MCP6541 is the backup if the common-mode limit causes problems during testing. The op-amp Schmitt trigger was rejected because it needs more parts and switches more slowly than a dedicated comparator.

docs.title: 3. 5 V Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
Subsystem: Board B – Cap / Lid Sensing (power)

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.STMicroelectronics L7805CV 5 V linear regulator (TO-220)$0.60/eachL7805CV at Mouser * Fixed 5 V output rated up to 1.5 A, far more than Board B needs* Built-in current limiting and thermal shutdown protect the board from wiring mistakes during bring-up* TO-220 through-hole package is easy to solder; at 100 mA from 9 V it dissipates only 0.4 W, so it needs no heatsink* Linear regulator as the course requires, stable with small input and output capacitors * About 2 V dropout means the input must stay above roughly 7 V, which rules out running long from a 9 V battery* Quiescent current of a few milliamps is wasted as heat* Only about 56 % efficient from a 9 V input (5 V / 9 V); the rest is lost as heat Solution Pros Cons Option 2.TI LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB 5 V low-dropout regulator (TO-220)$2.04/eachLM2940CT-5.0 at Mouser * Low dropout (0.5 V typical at 1 A) lets it keep regulating from a lower input voltage* Reverse-polarity protection (-15 V typical) survives a supply plugged in backwards* Over 1 A output in a TO-220 through-hole package * Needs an output capacitor of at least 22 µF with ESR between 0.1 Ω and 1 Ω, or it can oscillate* High quiescent current (10 mA typical at a 5 mA load), which is more than the sensor divider and comparator draw combined* More than three times the cost of Option 1 Solution Pros Cons Option 3.Microchip MCP1702-5002E/TO 5 V low-dropout regulator (TO-92)$0.65/eachMCP1702-5002E/TO at Mouser * Extremely low quiescent current (2 µA typical)* Low dropout (625 mV typical at 250 mA)* Stable with small 1 µF ceramic capacitors and takes up little board space * Rated for only 250 mA output, with little margin if more 5 V loads are added later* Maximum input voltage is 13.2 V, so there is little headroom for supply spikes or a higher-voltage adapter* TO-92 package cannot shed much heat: (9 V - 5 V) × 250 mA = 1 W, which is far too much for TO-92

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805CV

Rationale: Board B runs from a 9 V wall supply, so the L7805's 2 V dropout and few-milliamp quiescent current don't matter. 9 V leaves 4 V of headroom, twice the dropout. At Board B's low current the TO-220 package runs cool with no heatsink. Built-in current limiting and thermal shutdown protect the board during bring-up. It is also the least expensive option and is widely stocked. The LM2940 costs more than three times as much, has strict output-capacitor ESR limits, and draws more quiescent current, and its low-dropout advantage isn't needed with a 9 V input. The MCP1702 is limited to 250 mA and cannot dissipate the heat of a 4 V drop at higher currents.

docs.title: 4. Power Source
docs.text:
Subsystem: Board B – Cap / Lid Sensing (power)

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Adafruit 9 VDC 1000 mA regulated switching wall adapter$8.95/each9 V 1 A adapter at Adafruit * Regulated 9 V stays above the L7805's roughly 7 V minimum input while keeping regulator heat low* 5.5 mm / 2.1 mm center-positive plug mates with the PJ-102AH barrel jack on Board B* UL listed with a universal 100–240 VAC input* Gives continuous power to a dispenser that sits on a counter all day * Tied to a wall outlet, so the board does not run during a power outage* The most expensive item on Board B* Adafruit gives a specification list rather than a full manufacturer datasheet Solution Pros Cons Option 2.Adafruit 12 VDC 1000 mA regulated switching wall adapter$8.95/each12 V 1 A adapter at Adafruit * Same 5.5 mm / 2.1 mm center-positive plug, so it mates with the same barrel jack* More input headroom above the regulator's dropout* Regulated, UL listed, 1 A output * The L7805 must drop 7 V instead of 4 V, so it makes 75 % more heat for the same load current* Listed as out of stock at the time of writing, which risks the build schedule* Extra voltage brings no benefit, since nothing on Board B needs more than 5 V Solution Pros Cons Option 3.9 V alkaline battery (Energizer 522) with Adafruit 9 V battery clip and 5.5 mm / 2.1 mm plug$2.95/each (clip) + about $6.10/each (battery, Newark)9 V clip at Adafruit, Energizer 522 datasheet * Portable, with no outlet needed* The clip's center-positive barrel plug fits the same PJ-102AH jack, so no board change is needed* The clip is inexpensive and covers the battery terminals to prevent shorts * Small capacity (about 600 mAh), and the voltage falls below the L7805's roughly 7 V minimum input long before the battery is empty, so battery life is short* Batteries must be bought again and again* A dispenser that quietly loses power could miss a dose reminder, which defeats the purpose of the product

Choice: Option 1: Adafruit 9 VDC 1000 mA regulated wall adapter

Rationale: A pill dispenser stays in one place and must run reliably every day, so a wall adapter suits it better than a battery. A 9 V battery would drop below the L7805's minimum input early in its discharge. 9 V is the lowest standard adapter voltage that still clears the regulator's 2 V dropout with margin, so it keeps regulator heat lower than the 12 V adapter would. Its 1 A rating is far above what Board B draws. Its 5.5 mm / 2.1 mm plug mates with the PJ-102AH barrel jack already in the block diagram. It is regulated and UL listed, and it is in stock. The 12 V adapter is not.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Figure 1: Board B (Cap / Lid Sensing) subsystem schematic, Rev 3.

Board B detects when the pill bottle cap is opened. A photoresistor sits under the cap: with the cap closed it is dark, and when the cap opens light reaches it, its resistance drops and the divider voltage rises. The signal is amplified, filtered and read by the PIC's ADC, and an LM393 comparator also gives a clean open/closed signal. The board reports to the hub over the team's 8-pin ribbon cable.

Rev 3 (Oct 27): the DRV5055 Hall-effect sensor and cap magnet were replaced by a photoresistor (R18) and a 3.9 kΩ divider resistor (R19), as recommended by the teaching team. The gain, reference and comparator-threshold resistors were re-calculated for the new signal range. Everything else is unchanged from Rev 2.

docs.title: Amplified analog sensor
docs.text:
Stage Parts Design Sensor CdS photoresistor R18 (custom symbol LDR_AP, footprint AP_R_LDR_5.0x4.1mm_P3mm) + R19 = 3.9 kΩ to GND V = 3.3 × R19 / (R18 + R19): 0.26 V cap closed (46.3 kΩ dark), 0.86 V low light (11.07 kΩ), 2.37 V room light (1.54 kΩ) R19 choice Geometric mean of the lab readings √(11.07k × 1.54k) ≈ 4.1 kΩ → 3.9 kΩ standard value, maximizes the swing between low and room light Reference R8 = 120 kΩ / R9 = 10 kΩ divider, buffered by MCP6004 channel C VREF = 3.3 × 10k / 130k ≈ 0.25 V, set to the cap-closed level Gain MCP6004 channel A, non-inverting about VREF G = 1 + R3/R2 = 1 + 3.3k/10k ≈ 1.33, so ADC sees ≈ 0.26 V closed, 1.06 V low light, 3.07 V room light Low-pass filter R4 = 10 kΩ, C7 = 1 µF fc = 1 / (2π·R·C) ≈ 15.9 Hz Buffer MCP6004 channel B, unity gain Low-impedance drive into ADC pin RA0 Isolation JP2 (sensor), JP3 (ADC) Lets each stage be tested on its own

The photoresistor can sit on the board or next to the cap through header J4 (pin 1 = 3.3 V, pin 2 = LDR_OUT); R19 stays on the board.

docs.title: Debug and test features
docs.text:
• Heartbeat LED (D3, yellow) and lid status LED (D4, red), 330 Ω each: (3.3 − 2.0) / 330 ≈ 4 mA
  • Push button SW1 with 10k pull-up and 0.1 µF debounce capacitor
  • Test points TP1–TP9 on every power rail and every analog stage
  • Jumpers JP1–JP3 for isolating sections during debugging
  • Power expansion header J3 (VIN, 5 V, 3.3 V, GND)
  • 0.1 µF bypass capacitor on every power pin
  • Unused op-amp (U2D) and comparator (U5B) inputs tied off through 10k pull-up/pull-down resistors
  • Every capacitor lists a working voltage (≥25% margin) and every resistor a power rating (1/8 W, ≥50% margin)

Rev 2 passed ERC in KiCad 10 with 0 errors and 0 warnings. Rev 3 only changes the sensor parts and resistor values; its netlist was compared with Rev 2 and the only differences are U4 → R18/R19 and the HALL_OUT → LDR_OUT net name.

docs.title: How the schematic meets the product requirements
docs.text: User need / requirement Circuit that meets it Know when the cap is opened R18/R19 divider → LM393 comparator (with ≈ 69 mV hysteresis) → RB0 → LID_OPEN on ribbon pin 2 Analog signal chain into the ADC R18/R19 → U2A gain about VREF → R4/C7 15.9 Hz low-pass → U2B buffer → RA0 Detect a problem (sensor unplugged, dark room, cap never opened during a dose) Firmware compares the ADC level, comparator state and DOSE_READY and drives LID_FAULT on pin 3 Work with the rest of the dispenser 8-pin ribbon J1: DOSE_READY in, LID_OPEN / LID_FAULT / HEARTBEAT_B out, UART1 both ways Safe, reliable power 9 V adapter → 500 mA fuse → 1N5819 → L7805CV → 5 V VBUS (JP1); all analog on the Nano's 3.3 V rail Easy to test and debug TP1–TP9 on every rail and analog stage, JP1–JP3 isolation jumpers, heartbeat LED, debug button, expansion headers J3, J5–J7

docs.title: Power Budget
docs.text: Arya Padiyar | Team 102 | Board B: Cap / Lid Sensing | Rev 3

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Board B runs from a 9 V, 1 A wall adapter. The power path is 9 V adapter → 500 mA fuse + 1N5819 reverse-polarity diode → STMicroelectronics L7805CV → 5 V on the Curiosity Nano's VBUS (through jumper JP1) → the Nano's on-board MIC5353 LDO → 3.3 V for the PIC and every analog part. The budget below uses the course power budget template and the absolute maximum (worst-case) current of each part, with a 25 % safety margin on each rail.

Downloads: power budget spreadsheet (.xlsx) · PDF

docs.title: What the power budget showed
docs.text:
• Every rail has margin, even in the worst case. The tightest is the 3.3 V rail, where the PIC's 350 mA absolute maximum dominates. Even with that and a 25 % margin, the load stays under the Nano's 500 mA LDO. In normal operation the PIC draws a few milliamps, so the real margin is much larger.
  • The 9 V, 1 A adapter is more than enough. The worst-case draw is about 630 mA. The expected draw is roughly 15–30 mA (PIC, op-amp, comparator, two LEDs).
  • The L7805 needs no heatsink in normal use. At the expected load it dissipates about (9 − 5) × 0.03 ≈ 0.12 W. Only at the theoretical worst case (≈ 630 mA) would it reach ≈ 2.5 W and need a heatsink, which the TO-220 package allows if it is ever needed.
  • Changing to the photoresistor cut the sensor current. The LDR divider draws at most 0.83 mA (bright light) and about 0.07 mA with the cap closed.
  • Open question for the teaching team: Microchip documents VBUS only as an output, so feeding 5 V into it through JP1 should be confirmed before the board is built. JP1 must be removed whenever the Nano's USB cable is plugged in.

docs.title: Appendix
docs.text: Arya Padiyar | Team 102 | Board B: Cap / Lid Sensing

docs.title: A. Photoresistor measurements (Resistive Sensor Lab)
docs.text:
These are the photoresistor readings from the Resistive Sensor Lab. Board B's divider resistor, comparator threshold and gain stage are all calculated from them.

Light condition Measured resistance Divider output with R19 = 3.9 kΩ on 3.3 V Fully covered (cap closed) 46.3 kΩ 0.26 V Low indoor light 11.07 kΩ 0.86 V Fully lit room 1.54 kΩ 2.37 V Direct light / under a bulb 66.5 Ω 3.24 V

Divider resistor: R = √(R_low × R_room) = √(11.07 kΩ × 1.54 kΩ) ≈ 4.1 kΩ → 3.9 kΩ standard value.

Comparator threshold: 3.3 V × 10 kΩ / (51 kΩ + 10 kΩ) ≈ 0.54 V, between the closed (0.26 V) and dimmest open (0.86 V) readings.
